background.definition: CF is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by failure of the transmembrane regulator to control ion transport across the cell membrane. This results in abnormally viscid mucous secretions and leads to respiratory, gastrointestinal, and reproductive manifestations.

list.listitem: CF occurs in approximately 1 in 3000 Caucasian newborns. About 1 in 25 persons in the United States and UK is a carrier of the gene, and if two carriers mate, one in four children will be affected. It is much less common in persons of Asian and African descent.
CF affects about 30,000 people in the United States (about 70,000 worldwide).
CF is the most common life-threatening autosomal recessive disease in the United States and Europe.
CF is caused by one of over 1500 known cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene mutations. There are 24 common mutations that cause most cases of the disease.

The primary defect in the disease is abnormal function of an epithelial chloride channel protein encoded by the CFTR gene on chromosome band 7q31.2. The frequency of mutations in different populations is shown in .

Fluid secretion in exocrine glands and epithelial lining is affected, which leads to abnormally viscid mucous secretions, resulting in chronic lung disease, pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, malnutrition, hepatic cirrhosis, intestinal obstruction, and male infertility.

Chronic airway obstruction due to viscous secretions leads to colonization with pathogenic bacteria including H. influenzae, S. aureus, and P. aeruginosa. Persistent colonization and infection lead to an increase in inflammatory responses, thereby recruiting neutrophils, which promote tissue destruction via excessive release of elastase.
Pulmonary tissue destruction leads to bronchiectasis, decreased lung function, and respiratory failure.

A Cochrane review of two large RCTs with over 1 million neonates found that children with CF diagnosed in screened populations had improved nutritional and probably pulmonary outcomes. The CDC recommends that newborns be screened using a protocol that begins with a test for immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT). A
Infants with meconium ileus have a higher rate of false positive newborn screening for CF. B
If IRT is positive (elevated), perform diagnostic evaluation outlined in . C
ACIP guidelines recommend influenza vaccine for all CF patients 6 months of age or older, as well as close contacts of CF patients. Evidence from RCTs is lacking, though. C
While some guidelines recommend palivizumab as prophylaxis for RSV infections in infants with CF, an RCT with 186 infants found no benefit (one RSV infection in each group). B
Suspect CF in an infant with chronic or recurrent sinopulmonary, gastrointestinal, salt wasting, or genital abnormalities, as well as failure to thrive. C
Sweat chloride test and/or DNA testing are the recommended tests for confirmation of CF diagnosis; interpret using algorithm shown in . C
Initial diagnostic evaluation includes a careful history, pancreatic and hepatic function testing, CXR, and oropharyngeal cultures. C

Consider CF in patients presenting with chronic sinopulmonary disease, GI and nutritional abnormalities, salt loss syndromes, or genital abnormalities (males only). See below for specific manifestations.

Chronic or recurrent sinopulmonary disease: persistent or chronic colonization or infection with typical CF pathogens (Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa), chronic cough and sputum production, airway obstruction (wheezing or air trapping), nasal polyps, and digital clubbing.

Gastrointestinal and nutritional abnormalities: meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstruction syndrome, or rectal prolapse; pancreatic insufficiency or recurrent acute pancreatitis; prolonged neonatal jaundice or chronic liver disease; failure to thrive, hypoproteinemia, or edema; and complications secondary to fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies.
Salt loss syndromes: acute salt depletion and chronic metabolic alkalosis.
Genital abnormalities: congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens in males leading to obstructive azoospermia.

Patients may initially present with persistent chest radiograph abnormalities. Antenatal ultrasound may show fetal echogenic bowel indicating high suspicion of cystic fibrosis; however, this finding is not specific for CF.

If newborn screening is positive, obtain sweat chloride test and/or DNA testing for CFTR mutation(s) as described in "Approach to the patient" section (). The sweat chloride test is considered gold standard for confirmation of CF diagnosis.

Initial evaluation of the child diagnosed with CF includes the following: baseline height and weight, medical history, family history for CF, pancreatic function testing (below), culture of the oropharynx for pseudomonas and other pathogens commonly seen in CF patients, chest x-ray, and liver function tests. Current guidelines do not recommend CT, bronchoalveolar lavage, or pulmonary function testing in infants.

In patients diagnosed with CF, evaluate for pancreatic insufficiency using the monoclonal test for fecal elastase. A value <100 mcg/g in children over the age of 2 years is diagnostic for insufficiency. Serum trypsinogen is an alternative test, but only in older children (>7 years).
Consider bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage in infants with signs of infection who do not respond to therapy.
Any patient with signs or symptoms of CF should undergo sweat chloride testing and/or DNA testing for CFTR mutations.
See for a suggested diagnostic algorithm, based on Cystic Fibrosis foundation guidelines.
Patients diagnosed with CF should be referred to a center for complete evaluation and a treatment plan.
Care should be provided at an accredited cystic fibrosis care center, beginning within 3 days of diagnosis. C
Initiate pancreatic enzyme replacement in patients with evidence of pancreatic insufficiency. C

The combinations of lumacaftor-ivacaftor, tezacaftor-ivacaftor, or elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor are effective for reducing the risk of exacerbations, improving symptoms, and improving FEV1 in patients homozygous for Phe508del. A
Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor improves symptoms and FEV1 in patients with a single Phe508del allele and a second "minimal function" CFTR mutation. B
Providing chest physiotherapy and other forms of airway clearance are the standard of care, with some evidence of short-term benefits. A

In patients 6 years or older with chronic pseudomonas aeruginosa infection and moderate to severe lung disease, US and European guidelines recommend chronic use of inhaled tobramycin in alternate months to reduce exacerbations and improve lung function for patients with moderate-to-severe disease. A Cochrane review of 18 RCTs with 3042 participants concluded that inhaled tobramycin improves lung function and probably reduces the rate of exacerbations. For patients with chronic infection and mild lung disease, chronic use of inhaled tobramycin is also recommended but less strongly.

In patients 6 years or older with any degree of lung disease, chronic use of dornase alfa and inhaled tobramycin reduces exacerbations and improves lung function. In patients with moderate to severe lung disease it also improves quality of life. However, the timing of dornase alfa administration (before or after airway clearance) does not affect its degree of benefit.

Chronic use of inhaled hypertonic saline has been thought to reduce exacerbations and improve lung function in older children and adults. However, an RCT found that it did not improve outcomes in children under age 6 years during 48 weeks of follow-up, and a recent Cochrane review has called into question the efficacy of hypertonic saline in improving lung function even for older children and adults.
US guidelines recommend that chronic azithromycin should be considered for individuals 6 years and older who do not have pseudomonas aeruginosa chronically in airway cultures.
Efforts to eradicate MRSA or prophylactic anti-staphylococcal antibiotics are not recommended for asymptomatic infants.

Systematic reviews found insufficient evidence for the use of quarterly IV antibiotic prophylaxis for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. When treating a pulmonary exacerbation, a Cochrane review concluded based on 5 RCTs with 354 patients that aminoglycosides are as effective given once daily as they are given several times daily, with evidence that once-daily aminoglycosides causes less nephrotoxicity in children.
There is insufficient evidence regarding the need for treatment or efficacy of antibiotic combinations for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.
A Cochrane review found no RCT data to guide the duration of antibiotic therapy.
US guidelines recommend against the routine use of inhaled corticosteroids, prophylactic antistaphylococcal antibiotics, and chronic use of oral corticosteroids.

US guidelines found insufficient evidence regarding use of inhaled or oral N-acetylcysteine or glutathione, leukotriene modifiers, chronic use of oral antipseutomonal drugs, or inhaled anticholinergics.

European and US guidelines recommend lumacaftor-ivacaftor in patients with the Phe508del mutation. A placebo-controlled trial randomized 1108 patients and found significant improvements in FEV1, hospitalizations, and pulmonary exacerbations.

A randomized trial with 510 patients homozygous for the Phe508del gene found improvements in FEV1 and a lower rate of pulmonary exacerbations in the group randomized to tezacaftor-ivacaftor (0.64 vs 0.99 events per year; RR 0.65; 95% CI, 0.48-0.88). The drugs were well tolerated and safe.

A pair of randomized trials evaluated the transmembrane conductance regulator VX-445-tezacaftor-ivacaftor in patients with 1 or 2 Phe508del alleles and found good safety and improvements in FEV1, sweat chloride concentrations, and a disease specific symptom score.

An RCT identified 403 patients with a single Phe508del allele and a second "minimal function" CFTR mutation. They were randomized to tezacaftor-ivacaftor or elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor and followed for 24 weeks. The 3 drug combination resulted in higher FEV1, better symptom score, and lower sweat chloride concetrations. It was safe and generally well tolerated.

A cohort study used data from a US registry with up to 8 years follow-up to compare patients treated with ivacaftor with those who had not been treated. Treated patients had lower rates of mortality (HR 0.22, 95% CI 0.09-0.45), hospitalization (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.43-0.56) and lung transplant (HR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02-0.28).

listitem.em: Other medications to reduce the risk of exacerbations

list.listitem: A Cochrane review of 3 RCTs concluded that chronic use of high dose oral ibuprofen slows the loss of lung function in patients with FEV1 >60% predicted.
Inhaled mannitol twice daily for 2 weeks improves pulmonary function in patients with mild-to-moderate CF, but the impact on clinical outcomes is not known.

Data from RCTs are insufficient regarding bronchodilators and leukotriene inhibitors, but the former in particular are routinely used in patients with wheeze and demonstrable airway hyperresponsiveness.
Inhaled corticosteroids provide no benefit in patients with CF and should not be used.
Topical short-acting sodium channel blockers provide no benefit in patients with CF and may lead to deterioration in lung function.
Treating acute respiratory exacerbations: See "Complications" section below.
In infants under 2 years, initiate therapy in infants with signs of malabsorption or fecal elastase <200 mcg/g.

For children and adults, the CF Foundation guidelines recommend the following for pancreatic insufficiency: 500 to 2,500 units lipase per kg body weight per meal; or <10,000 units lipase per kg body weight per day; or <4,000 units lipase per gram dietary fat per day.

Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is present in about a third of adults with CF, due to long-term and frequent steroid use. A systematic review combining data from 9 studies with 385 participants found that bisphosphonates increase bone density, but with no evidence of reduced fracture rates. However, the latter is probably due to lack of sample size and limited follow-up (typically 2 years).
Nasal polyps: A systematic review of topical steroids to treat nasal polyps only found one small trial with 46 patients; no benefit was seen.
Liver disease: There are no data regarding use of ursodeoxycholic acid.

Growth: A post-hoc analysis found that ivacaftor may increase height and weight growth velocity in pre-pubescent children with CF compared with placebo (compared with placebo growth velocity: Height: 1.08 cm/y (p <0.05); Weight 3.11 kg/year; (p <0.001)).

Gastric acidity: Symptoms related to increased gastric acidity are common in persons with CF. A Cochrane review identified 17 small, low quality RCTs with 273 participants and could draw no clear conclusions regarding efficacy of acid reducing drugs.

Lung transplantation may be considered for CF patients with progressive lung impairment, severe hypoxemia, and hypercarbia who experience increasing functional impairment. Increasing antibiotic resistance and frequent or life-threatening pulmonary complications (such as massive hemoptysis) are another indication.
Long-term results are improving, with high volume centers now reporting 10 year mean survival.

Surgical and chemical pleurodesis should be considered for patients with recurrent episodes of clinically significant pneumothorax. Clinical trials are lacking, although experts generally prefer surgical over chemical pleurodesis.
A systematic review found 4 studies with 91 patients looking at omega-3 fatty acids. They found some physiologic changes, but no data regarding clinical outcomes.
Systematic reviews do not support use of antioxidant supplements, vitamin A supplementation, vitamin D supplementation, or the use of antibiotic adjuvants such as zinc, garlic, or beta-carotene.
Manually assisted cough should be considered in patients with expiratory muscle weakness to reduce the incidence of respiratory complications.
Autogenic drainage should be taught as an adjunct to postural drainage as a method to clear sputum because of its advantage of being performed without assistance and in one position.

Airway clearance of some kind is typically recommended and is thought to provide at least short-term benefits regarding symptoms and lung function. A Cochrane review found that patients who used PEP (positive expiratory pressure) physiotherapy had fewer pulmonary exacerbations than patients who used other forms of chest physiotherapy (active cycle of breathing techniques, autogenic drainage, oral oscillating PEP devices, high frequency chest wall oscillation, BiPAP, and exercise). However, there was no difference in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) among patients who used different forms of chest physiotherapy.

A systematic review of 6 RCTs involving 348 participants showed that physical training appears to improve exercise capacity. However, there was minimal benefit to lung function and health-related quality of life. There is insufficient evidence regarding the efficacy of inspiratory muscle training.

"Active Cycle of Breathing Technique" is intended to improve clearance of mucus. In 8 RCTs with 259 participants it appears to be comparable to other approaches to chest physiotherapy, such as airway oscillating devices or high-frequency chest compression. It may be more acceptable to patients than these alternatives, though.
A Cochrane review found that non-invasive ventilation may be a useful adjunct to other airway clearance techniques, with an improvement in exercise performance in one small study.

A Cochrane review of 24 RCTs with 875 participants concluded that active training programs provide a small improvement in exercise capacity, although there was little or no efect on quality of life or lung function parameters.
Be aware of the significant psychological burden of dealing with a chronic illness such as CF, and be prepared to provide or refer for appropriate counseling if necessary.

Breastfeeding is recommended for infants under 2 years. For children >2 years of age and adults, the CF Foundation recommends energy intakes greater than the standard for the general population with calorie dense food to support weight maintenance in adults and weight gain at an age-appropriate rate in children.

An RCT of the home-based nutrition education program "Eat Well With CF" showed no overall weight difference between intervention and control group at 6 or 12 months. There were no significant differences in FEV1 between the groups at 6 or 12 months.
Oral protein calorie supplementation is widely recommended, but good studies are lacking and the existing studies are inconclusive.
While used in clinical practice, a Cochrane review found no clinical trials of enteral tube feedings for patients with CF.
Instruct family members regarding proper handwashing and avoidance of respiratory secretion exchange when coughing.
Minimize contact between CF patients to avoid transmission of pathogens common to these patients but otherwise uncommon in the community.
Home IV antibiotic therapy for patients with an infection are an option. One small RCT found that it was safe and effective, and costs were lower than hospital-based therapy.
Oxygen therapy is commonly used in patients with more advanced stages of CF, especially at night.

A Cochrane review of topical gene replacement therapy with cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance gene replacement found one study where liposome-based CFTR gene replacement therapy was associated with improved lung function, but no improvement in quality of life, decreased disease burden, or decreased number of CF flare-ups.
There are no clear guidelines on the optimum duration of IV antibiotic treatment. Duration of treatment is currently based on unit policies and response to treatment.
Continue chronic therapies unless there is a specific contraindication; regarding inhaled antibiotics in particular, evidence is insufficient, while airway clearance therapies should be increased.
The most common pathogens are staph aureus and pseudomonas aeruginosa, as well as burkholderia cepacia, stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and achromobacter species.

Empiric therapy with two antipseudomonal antibiotics is the standard of care. However, the supporting evidence for combination therapy over monotherapy is poor. A Cochrane review identified 8 RCTs with 356 participants (mostly from the 1970's and 1980's) and concluded that there was no clear advantage of two antibiotics over one.
There is no clear optimal duration for antibiotic therapy. Routine use of synergy testing (to determine an optimal pair of antibiotics based on resistance patterns) is not recommended.
Routine use of corticosteroids is not recommended.
Intravenous antibiotics should not be delivered in a nonhospital setting unless resources and support equivalent to the hospital setting can be assured (eg. optimized airway clearance and nutrition).
Hospitalize patients with large pneumothorax, place a chest tube, and consider pleurodesis in those with previous episodes of pneumothorax.
After an episode, patients should not fly on a plane, lift more than 5 pounds, or do incentive spirometry for at least 2 weeks.
Patients with more than 5 mL of hemoptysis should seek care. Hospital admission is generally not required for those with scant hemoptysis.
Treat with antibiotics as this may be a sign of pulmonary infection.
Stop NSAIDs and bilevel positive airway pressure until the episode has resolved.
Consider bronchial artery embolization for patients with massive hemoptysis.

The cumulative probability of survival at 20 and 30 years of age was 80.4% and 63%, respectively. The median survival age was 38 years in a 2002 study, but is probably increasing. Survival was not significantly different between males and females. B
The CF-ABLE Score helps predict likelihood of death or lung transplant in adults with cystic fibrosis. B
Digestive tract cancers (standardized incidence ratio 3.5), testicular cancer (SIR 1.7), and lymphoid leukemia (SIR 2.0) are more common, while melanoma is less common. B
